description:
We are a multidisciplinary team of passionate innovators interested in space exploration, artificial intelligence, software development, and emerging technologies. We love transforming ambitious ideas into creative, functional solutions with real-world impact.

We welcome curious, collaborative individuals with skills in programming, UI/UX design, data science, engineering, research, or storytelling. Above all, we value creativity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn!
summary: MARS OS is a layered, integrated map a Mars astronaut could use to plan and carry out a Marswalk safely while doing new science. It answers the questions a survival guide must answer: where can we land, where is the water, what is dangerous, how do we move, and what does a mission need to stay alive? It brings data from 20+ NASA missions and datasets onto one globe you can fly from orbit to boot level. Every NASA robot that reached the surface is on the map with its real path, stops, photos, findings and sounds. Water-ice evidence, minerals, dune fields and NASA's candidate Exploration Zones for human missions show resources and hazards. Routes for rovers and astronauts are compared on measured slopes, with risk warnings and a downloadable route sheet. In the Mission Lab, anyone can drop a crew, rover or base anywhere and see oxygen, energy, Earth light time, radiation and EVA range, then ask Gemini whether the mission answers its question. Every number shows its source, and nothing changes the map without human approval. Robots explore Mars today; MARS OS turns what they learned into a map future crews can trust.
details:
What it does

MARS OS is a layered map a Mars astronaut could use to plan and carry out a Marswalk safely while doing new science, a survival guide in map form. It layers optical, thermal, spectral, topographic, atmospheric and radiation data from multiple NASA missions, and includes a helmet-visor HUD view. It helps a planner or a future crew answer five questions with real data:

  1. Where can we land? The Landing tab explains how landing sites are chosen, shows real landing ellipses (InSight's computes to 129.6 × 27.0 km from the NASA polygon; NASA states 130 × 27 km) and the 51 Exploration Zones NASA collected for the first human missions. Pin any point to get a factual check: elevation, latitude, slope, nearest ice, minerals, nearest robot and nearest zone.
  2. Where is the water and what resources exist? Craters that exposed water ice (Dundas et al. 2014) and 1,309 buried glaciers, 6,220 orbital mineral detections, and Perseverance's 30 named rock samples with NASA photos and the camera views inside each tube.
  3. What is dangerous? Mapped dune fields (the sand that trapped Spirit), steep slopes, low-resolution data and ground no rover has ever crossed are flagged on every route.
  4. How do we move? Shortest vs. gentlest route for a rover (Perseverance's 24° tilt limit) or an astronaut, on measured slopes. You can load a real Perseverance drive and compare it, read "why this route" (data used and data missing), simulate the drive with a 3D rover and download a route sheet with sources.
  5. What does a mission need? The Mission Lab: drop a crew, rover or base anywhere, even against MARS OS's advice. It computes oxygen (NASA BVAD), energy (sunlight by latitude, season and dust; solar area vs. MMRTGs), communication with Earth (distance, light time and solar conjunction from JPL orbital elements), radiation (MSL RAD vs. NASA's career limit), water distance and EVA range. It compares two base sites and asks Gemini whether the mission answers its question, using only those facts.

Every robot, every expedition.

All NASA surface missions from Viking 1 to Ingenuity, with photos, findings, instruments, official links, NASA videos and Mars sounds, 66 expedition stops with NASA descriptions, Curiosity's and Perseverance's full drives and raw photos per stop (loaded live), and 3D rover models where each rover is today. Near a real stop, the visor HUD shows "Perseverance was here" with the photos the rover took there.

A map that can change without being falsified.

Every region has a stable ID and an editable grid. A person or Gemini can propose a terrain correction with evidence; it is validated, kept pending until a person approves it, and stored in a reversible version history.

How it works

  • Front end: React, TypeScript, Three.js / React Three Fiber, a quadtree level-of-detail globe streaming NASA Mars Trek tiles, multi-resolution elevation (MOLA 14.8 km global grid, 463 m loaded on demand anywhere, CTX 20 m at Jezero), Mars24 sun position.
  • Live NASA feeds: MMGIS traverses (Perseverance, Curiosity, Ingenuity), raw-image APIs, MEDA and REMS weather, Mars Trek ArcGIS services, NASA Image and Video Library.
  • Backend (Node.js on Render): Gemini API with schema-validated answers, rate limits and no silent fallback; on-demand MOLA elevation.
  • Data contract in Zod with JSON Schemas, bilingual interface (English and Spanish).

Why it is valid

We checked our numbers against NASA: landing coordinates against hardware located in HiRISE images (we corrected Pathfinder by 21.6 km and InSight by 16.3 km), MOLA vs. rover elevation at Jezero (−2568 m vs. −2569.9 m), our sunrise/sunset vs. MEDA (within 10 s), our Earth–Mars model vs. the 2025 opposition (0.644 vs. 0.642 AU). Every value is labelled measured, derived or modelled, with its source.

Impact

Robots explore Mars today, and each one was sent to a different place. MARS OS joins what they learned with what orbiters mapped, so students, planners and future crews can see where Mars is known, where it is not, and what a mission there would need.
